title: Web Framework Landscape: Gin vs Echo vs Fiber vs Chi

scenes.heading: Gin vs Echo vs Fiber vs Chi
scenes.narration: Go has no single blessed web framework, so let's map the whole landscape from thin routers to batteries-included frameworks.

scenes.heading: A spectrum, not a winner
items: Chi and the stdlib mux stay pure net/http
Gin and Echo add ergonomic contexts and middleware
Fiber is fastest but runs on fasthttp, not net/http
scenes.narration: Think of it as a dial rather than a contest. At one end, the standard library mux and Chi never leave the http.Handler world, so the entire ecosystem plugs straight in. In the middle, Gin and Echo trade the standard handler signature for their own ergonomic Context with binding and rich middleware. At the far end, Fiber abandons net/http entirely for fasthttp to win raw benchmarks.

scenes.text: fasthttp is not net/http, so standard middleware and libraries don't work with Fiber.
scenes.narration: Here is the single most important fact. Because Fiber sits on fasthttp, its handler receives a fiber Context, not an http.Request or http.ResponseWriter. That means the whole standard func-of-http.Handler middleware ecosystem, plus libraries like OpenTelemetry and oauth2, simply do not work with it.

scenes.heading: One route, four handler signatures
scenes.narration: Watch the same route diverge across four stacks. The standard mux and Chi both take an http.ResponseWriter and a request pointer, so a handler written for one works on the other unchanged. Gin hands you its own Context, and Fiber hands you a fiber Context backed by fasthttp. Only the first two speak native net/http and stay reusable across the standard ecosystem.

scenes.heading: How to choose
steps: Default to the Go 1.22 stdlib mux
Step up to Chi for route groups
Reach for Gin or Echo for built-in ergonomics
Pick Fiber only for latency-critical edge services
scenes.narration: So how do you decide? Start with the standard library mux, which since Go one twenty-two supports method and wildcard patterns with zero dependencies. Step up to Chi when you want nested route groups while staying net/http compatible. Choose Gin or Echo when built-in binding and curated middleware clearly earn their weight. And reach for Fiber only for latency-critical, low-logic services where you accept leaving the standard ecosystem behind.

scenes.text: Routing is rarely the bottleneck — choose on compatibility and maintainability, not benchmarks.
scenes.narration: The bottom line: routing is order path-length and negligible next to your database, network calls, and serialization. So choose primarily on net/http compatibility, ecosystem reuse, and long-term maintainability, not on a synthetic hello-world throughput number.
